newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Chechens cling to myth that Dudayev lives.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chechens cling to myth that Dudayev lives.

text.p: Ask a Chechen whether Dzhokhar Dudayev, their former charismatic leader, is alive and he will say: "Of course he is".
Ask a Chechen when Dudayev will return, he will smile enigmatically and say: "Well, you know...," and leave the sentence unfinished.
A legend now surrounds Dudayev, who declared independence from Russia in 1991 and led the fight against Moscow after Russian troops attacked in late 1994.

He was reported killed in a Russian rocket attack in April this year, but his body was spirited away by a few close aides and details of his death, said to have occurred as he spoke on a satellite telephone, are murky.

At the time few Chechens believed he had died, even though a series of wakes were held. Journalists have not seen his grave or a videotape of a funeral said to have been held. Five months without him have done little to change their minds.

"He (Dudayev) will appear again, he cannot but appear," said one Chechen woman at recent celebrations for the fifth anniversary of Dudayev's independence declaration at this small village, near a shrine to earlier independence fighters.
The Dudayev legend is fuelled by a desire for an almost supernatural hero, who has outwitted death as well as the Russians.
It is part of a culture of myths, spiced with a sense of humour, which includes the idea Chechnya will one day be linked somehow to England, which will "save" it from the Russians.

There were strong rumours that Dudayev would appear at the fifth anniversary events, coming as they did after a peace agreement between Kremlin envoy Alexander Lebed and rebel commander Aslan Maskhadov, designed to end the 21-month war.
But Dudayev did not show up.

Many people carried large placards with Dudayev's portrait, showing his slim face, trademark moustache and army cap. Many Chechens have photographs of their late leader stuck to their car windscreens.
Chechens point out that Dudayev's body was never found and say he went abroad to seek treatment for his injuries.
They point to Chechen field commander Salman Raduyev, supposedly killed in March but who later made a dramatic return, his face altered beyond recognition by plastic surgery.
They also recall Imam Shamil, who fought against Tsarist Russia for decades and disappeared for a time only to return. He eventually capitulated to Russia in 1859.

But sometimes when Chechens say Dudayev is alive, the impression is they do not really believe he is alive but want to perpetuate a national joke, one which has become part of their resistance against the Russians.

"We heard that he went to Germany, to a NATO base, to be cured, then to America and is now in Turkey," said Abdul Viskiev, reciting one of the versions of Dudayev's fate that has circulated in local newspapers.
He was certain Dudayev would come back and said current Chechen president, Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, would resume his former post of vice-president when Dudayev returned.
But Sultan Mustiyev hinted Dudayev was more of a symbol than a living presence, although he also refused to say openly he thought he was dead.
"Dudayev will stay in the hearts and minds of all our people and he will stay as a symbol," he said.
But he then added: "We do not doubt that he is alive."
The Dudayev myth circulates along with one on "Angliya" often used to mean Britain as well as just England.
Many Chechens say England will one day save their region from Russian aggression.

"Our forefathers foretold this war with Russia, they said it would last two years and that soon after there would be another war," said Viskiev, whose words were greeted with nods of agreement by Chechens all around him.
"After that, England will take us for seven years and look after us," he added.
Where this myth about England came from, no-one seemed to know.

Some Chechens said it may be from the time Great Britain was worried over Tsarist Russia's imperial ambitions or when British oil companies were prospecting in Chechnya in the early years of this century.
"My grandfather still has shares bought in English oil companies," Mustiyev said. "Our forefathers said investment here will be by English people."
